text: Real strategies rarely rely on just one signal. A momentum signal, a value signal, a quality signal each capture something different, and a good blend can be more robust than any one alone — but combining badly is one of the easiest ways to quietly let a bad signal ruin a good one.

You measure a signal's quality with the information coefficient, or IC — the correlation between the signal at a point in time and the forward return it's actually trying to predict. It sounds small, but in cross-sectional equity signals an IC of two to eight percent is genuinely useful; this is a game of small, repeatable edges, not big single calls.

The simplest way to combine normalized signals is equal weighting, which is simple and hard to overfit. A more deliberate option weights each signal by its own measured IC, so a stronger signal counts for more. Either way, check the correlation between your candidate signals first — two highly correlated signals aren't two independent votes, they're mostly the same vote counted twice.

Concretely, IC weighting takes each signal's measured information coefficient, normalizes those into weights that sum to one, and blends the signals accordingly, so the stronger one naturally carries more influence.

One honest caveat: estimating those weights from the same history you'll judge the result on is itself a form of parameter fitting, the same risk chapter four covers for any backtest. Validate combination weights out of sample before trusting them. Up next, lesson eight: turning a combined signal into actual portfolio weights.
